newsitem.title: USA: Unabomber case judge rules for prosecution on notes.
newsitem.headline: Unabomber case judge rules for prosecution on notes.

text.p: A U.S. magistrate issued a tentative ruling on Monday that prosecutors do not have to turn over investigators' handwritten notes to lawyers for Unabomber suspect Theodore Kaczynski.

Kaczynski's lawyers had filed a motion asking U.S. Magistrate Gregory Hollows to order prosecutors to give them copies of notes made by FBI agents during their search of the reclusive former mathematics professor's Montana cabin in April. Kaczynski is accused of being the shadowy Unabomber who killed three people and injured 23 during an anti-technology bombing campaign between 1978 and 1995.

At a court hearing in Sacramento, Judy Clarke, an attorney for Kaczynski, said the notes might show whether there had been any "contamination" of the evidence seized at the cabin. But prosecutor Stephen Freccero said the prosecution had already turned over a lot of evidence to the defence and had decided to "draw the line" at the handwritten notes.

"We feel it's important, six months into this case, to draw the line somewhere, because this will just be the beginning," Freccero said. He said the handwritten logs detailed which investigators were at the cabin and showed for example that at one stage an explosives team was brought in.

Clarke said the notes dealt with the "chain of custody" of evidence seized at the cabin and could go to the heart of the government's case against Kaczynski. "What I find sort of remarkable is that the government simply doesn't want to give this (to the defence)," she said.

After the 15-minute hearing, Hollows said his tentative decision was that the notes were not material to Kaczynski's defence, meaning the government would not have to turn them over. But he said he would think about the legal arguments and issue his final, written ruling by the end of the week.
Kaczynski, 54, held in a Sacramento jail, was not present at Monday's hearing, having waived his right to attend.

The Harvard-educated Kaczynski was arrested at his Montana cabin in April and transferred two months later to Sacramento where he has been charged with four of the bombings, two of them deadly. He has pleaded not guilty. The government has not yet announced if it will seek the death penalty.
He has been indicted separately in New Jersey on charges that he mailed a bomb that killed advertising executive Thomas Mosser in December 1994.

Prosecutors and investigators have said they found extensive evidence at the cabin incriminating Kaczynski, including bomb components and a diary that they say contained his "detailed admission" to each of the 16 Unabomber attacks.

In papers filed before the hearing, Kaczynski's lawyers asked the magistrate to force the government to turn over documents they said they needed to prepare a motion challenging the validity of the warrant obtained by the FBI to search Kaczynski's cabin. Prosecutors are required to share with defence lawyers any evidence that might be useful in preparing an accused's defence.
A pre-trial hearing in the case is scheduled to be held in Sacramento on Friday at which U.S. District Judge Garland Burrell may set a date for the start of the trial.
